# CloudBitmaps

> Distributed, cloud-native Roaring Bitmaps. Query and intersect large integer sets straight out of
> object storage — a bounded RAM cache over immutable `.crbm` generations in your own bucket — at a fraction
> of an always-on cache, with the familiar bitmap API: `has`, `count`, `iterate`, `intersect`, `union`,
> `andNot`. Ids are unsigned 32-bit integers.

## A first example

Save as a `.mjs` file (the packages are ESM-only, Node 22.12 or later) after `pnpm add @cloudbitmaps/roaring`:

```js
import { CloudRoaring, MemoryStorage } from '@cloudbitmaps/roaring';

// For S3 instead: import { S3Storage } from '@cloudbitmaps/s3'; storage: new S3Storage({ bucket: 'my-bitmaps' })
const store = new CloudRoaring({ storage: new MemoryStorage() });

await store.load({ segment: 'shoppers' }, [5, 99_999, 1_234_567_890]); // a load replaces the segment
await store.load({ segment: 'active' }, [5, 7, 1_234_567_890]);

const shoppers = store.segment('shoppers');
console.log(await shoppers.has(99_999), await shoppers.count()); // true 3
for await (const id of shoppers.intersect([store.segment('active')])) console.log(id); // 5, then 1234567890
```

CloudBitmaps maps each 16-bit Roaring chunk onto pluggable cloud storage: an in-process LRU cache over a storage
tier of write-once `.crbm` generations, with one small registry row per segment saying which generation is
current. The distinguishing capability is **serverless chunk-skipping intersection**: `A ∩ B` fetches only the
chunks that can possibly contribute, so intersecting two 2,000,000-id segments touches only the shared chunks,
and `count()` on a published segment does zero payload reads.

Install two packages: a codec and a storage — `pnpm add @cloudbitmaps/roaring @cloudbitmaps/s3` (or `npm i` the
same two). `@cloudbitmaps/core` (the codec-agnostic engine, the `.crbm` format and the storage interfaces) is a
dependency of both and is never installed directly; it contains no cloud SDK at all. Four storage backends: S3
(`@cloudbitmaps/s3`, which also serves an S3-compatible store such as R2 or MinIO, given its endpoint, if it
honours S3's conditional writes; MinIO is the one the integration suite runs against), GCS (`@cloudbitmaps/gcs`)
and Azure Blob (`@cloudbitmaps/azure-blob`) as packages of their own, each depending on its cloud SDK for real
rather than as an optional peer, and the local filesystem (`LocalFsStorage`, from `@cloudbitmaps/roaring`, for
development); plus the in-memory `MemoryStorage`, also from `@cloudbitmaps/roaring`, for tests. Each of the three clouds hosts both the storage generations and the registry, so a
deployment needs exactly one cloud account.

A store is wired with ONE backend object — `new CloudRoaring({ storage: new S3Storage({ bucket }) })` — which
carries both the generations and the currentGen pointer, from one bucket and one prefix. MemoryStorage
and LocalFsStorage come from the flavor's main entry; S3Storage, GcsStorage and AzureBlobStorage from
`@cloudbitmaps/s3`, `@cloudbitmaps/gcs` and `@cloudbitmaps/azure-blob` respectively. There is no separate
`registry` option.

## How data gets in

Only by loading a whole new generation. `store.load(ref, ids)` writes one immutable object, checks the result is
plausible (an empty result over a non-empty segment is refused, reported as `published: false` with a `reason`),
moves the pointer to it by a compare-and-swap fenced on the registry row it read, and collects what the move
superseded, keeping one generation below the new pointer. It takes an array, a Set or an async cursor. A backend
(MemoryStorage / LocalFsStorage / S3Storage / GcsStorage / AzureBlobStorage) carries both the generations and the pointer and is what
`storage` normally takes; a hand-written `{ storage, registry }` object is refused. `storage` also accepts a
bare `IStorageDriver` (a storage driver, not a backend), which has no registry, so the store is read-only and cleartext; or an already-built
StorageChunkSource for advanced reader wiring, which is read-only too and reads with whatever registry and
keystore it was built with. A driver author who wants a storage and a registry of their own — an instrumented storage, a registry
elsewhere — pairs them with `brandAsBackend({ storage, registry })` from `@cloudbitmaps/core/driver-kit`.
Nothing mutates a stored bitmap, so a crash before the publish leaves the previous generation authoritative, a rerun is idempotent, and there is no partially-visible write. There is
no per-id write. `intersectInto`/`unionInto`/`andNotInto` use the same protocol, publishing their result as a
new generation of the destination segment — and check the result is plausible the same way `load` does: an empty
or implausible combine over a non-empty destination is refused (`published: false` + `reason`) rather than
wiping it, with `allowEmpty`/`guard` to override. Unlike `load` they collect nothing by default, so a rollback
target survives a materialization.

Every chunk a read fetches is whole and checksum-verified, from one generation, resolved once before any
fan-out; a long read can move to a newer generation part-way (a `cache.genTtlMs` refresh, an eviction, a sweep,
an invalidation), and `seg.pin()` holds one generation for as long as a job needs it. The reads: has (cache,
else one ranged GET once the segment's pointer and index are read), count (exact, from the registry row's summary,
one request when cold, else summed from the .crbm index, with zero payload reads), iterate, and the composites — intersect and andNot, which skip every chunk that cannot
contribute, and union, which reads every chunk of every operand — with `exclude` suppression folded into the
same pass. A combine refuses an operand that names no segment (`ValidationError`) rather than reading it as
empty, unless `allowAbsentOperands: true`. `iterate`, `intersect`, `union` and `andNot` return a stream you `for await` one id at a time, or call `.batches()` on for one `Uint32Array` per chunk (the same ids, ascending). An id-range read, `iterate({ after, through })` and the same options
on every combine, yields only the ids in (after, through] and fetches only the chunks the range overlaps.

## Measured, expected and modelled

Counts come from running the engine; prices are the default list prices. With the pointer in the same bucket as the
data, the topology that ships: a cold intersect of two 500,000-id segments sharing 100 of their 1,999 chunks is expected,
and not yet measured on S3, to make 6 GETs, $2.40 per million, reading neighbouring chunks as ranges; on a spread layout
it reads more bytes than it needs, which cross-region can cost more than the requests it saves. Measured against real S3
in us-east-1, with the request counts read off the AWS SDK layer: a segment's first store.load() is 2 PUTs and 4 GETs,
$11.60 per million, and a cold count() is one request at 27.82 ms (run of 2026-10-04 from AWS CloudShell inside the
region, whose client had 50 sockets; the client this release builds allows 128, and its effect is not measured). For
comparison: an always-on Redis-HA line of $346/month standing, and a modelled $0.03/month for 1.2 GiB of segments at
rest. One crossover is published, in GETs: past 329.15 sustained GETs a second, with every read missing the cache,
metered GETs pass the standing cluster — a warmer cache moves that line up. For cold intersects of the shape above, at
their expected 6 GETs each, that line is 54.9 /s intersects a second.

## Coming from Redis bitmaps

A durable home for set-shaped work — audiences, dedup, suppression, membership, eligibility — where the sets are
large, mostly read, must survive a restart, and are computed in batches upstream. The read side maps
one-for-one: GETBIT/BITCOUNT become has/count, BITOP AND/OR/DIFF become intersect/union/andNot, and intersect
skips the chunks that cannot contribute. You are not giving up the bitmap either: past 4,096 ids in a 65,536-id
chunk (6.25% of it) Roaring stores that chunk as a flat bit array, one bit per possible id, unless the ids run
contiguously, when it stores runs. Not the same bytes as a Redis bitmap, though: Redis numbers a byte's bits
from the most significant, and Roaring packs a chunk's bits into 64-bit words from the least.

Not a drop-in replacement, and the two limits are load-bearing rather than footnotes:

1. No per-id write, and that is the difference. SETBIT has no equivalent: a segment changes only by publishing
   a new generation, so a SETBIT loop has nothing to port to. If the set is defined by a query, run the query
   and load the result; if it is defined by events arriving one at a time, accumulate them where they arrive
   (Redis is genuinely good at that) and load the set on a cadence. A load bills per object, not per id — ten
   million ids are a handful of PUTs. Removing one id everywhere is a compliance operation (eraseSubject, a
   generation rewrite), not a hot-path verb.
2. No addressable-bit surface. BITPOS, BITFIELD, byte-range BITCOUNT and BITOP NOT have no equivalent — this is
   a set of ids, not a positional bit buffer, and NOT has no bounded universe to complement against. The raw
   bytes are not interoperable either: a .crbm object is not a flat bit array, and raw bit-position import is
   not built.

Retention is per segment and built in: setRetention(ref, {expiresAt}) records when a segment becomes eligible
for retirement, and retireExpired() is the sweep that acts on it, retiring each expired segment through
dropSegment. The expiry is an absolute instant the writer sets, not a duration derived from anything observed,
because every load rewrites the basis such a duration would use. The sweep is a function you schedule -- this
library starts no timer, so the sweep behaves the same in a Lambda and in a long-running server. (An edge
isolate runs none of it: the roaring codec is a native addon, which no isolate can load.) A handle can also
carry its own deadline, store.segment(name, { expiresAt }), and reads empty past it with no I/O; that reclaims
nothing and binds that handle alone. There is no per-id TTL: a bitmap stores ids, not timestamps, and a per-id
timestamp costs more than the compression saves.

## No background process, and nothing to seed

There is no daemon and no lifecycle worker. A segment exists once a generation has been loaded into it -- there
is no create verb, segment(name) is just a validated address that does no I/O, and exists(ref) /
segments({namespace}) ask the registry what is there rather than you keeping your own list of names beside the
store. The only scheduled work is the retention sweep above (a load collects the generations it supersedes itself, and an
*Into does when given keep; neither touches the current generation). An operator can move a pointer back with
store.rollback(ref, generation), to a generation still in the bucket (store.generations(ref) lists them); it
deletes nothing. Compliance is built in: subjectReport (Art. 15) and eraseSubject (Art. 17 -- a generation
rewrite that deletes the generation holding the bit, so for every segment its ledger reports `erased: true` the
bit is physically gone from the bucket when the call returns), both scoped by a `namespace` or
`{ allNamespaces: true }`; dropSegment; checkConsistency; exportSegments -- eject every segment to portable roaring or ndjson,
which is the exit path; and the crypto-shred free functions destroySegment and eraseNamespace, which take the
backend's registry rather than the store, so a store beside them is told with store.invalidate(ref).

## When NOT to use it

If you need a sub-millisecond p99, use Redis. Our cache is in-process RAM, so on a hit there is nothing between
us; the limit is the tail: a check that misses the cache costs a ranged GET against object storage, where an
in-process RAM store costs a memory read. CloudBitmaps is for sets that are large, mostly read, and shouldn't
cost $346/month to keep warm. The in-region run of 2026-10-04 measured a cold count() at 27.82 ms.

## Status

v0.14.0, Apache-2.0, published tokenlessly with SLSA build provenance. Pre-1.0: breaking changes are possible in
a minor bump until the .crbm format freezes at 1.0.
